Tori Trades' two-line trendline method, as coded in ../../../projects/trading experiments/tori_trendline_lab.pine (TradingView strategy "Tori Trendline Lab") and tested in that folder and in ../../../projects/trading-equation-backtests/. Education, not investment advice.

0. Her actual process is top-down (sections 2–5 below are only the lower-timeframe part)

Sources agree on the shape, not every detail (no official full write-up found): Chart Fanatics / Tradezella playbook pages, a summary of the Chart Fanatics video, and TradingView scripts modelled on the method.

  1. Higher timeframes first (monthly → weekly → daily): find the main trend from market structure — higher highs + higher lows = uptrend, lower highs + lower lows = downtrend — and mark the big swing highs/lows and support/resistance levels. This sets the bias: which direction to trade.
  2. Drop to the execution chart (4-hour): draw thick, hand-adjusted trendlines (not snapped to exact wicks) with 2–3+ touches, at least ~1 week of data from the first touch to the entry. Mark the Action Line and the Safety Line.
  3. Take only setups that agree with the higher-timeframe bias:
    • Bounce off a trendline that runs with the higher-timeframe trend, or
    • Break of a short counter-trend line (e.g. weekly/daily uptrend → 4H pullback makes a falling line → price breaks it → the big trend resumes). Needs a clear Safety Line close by; skip if it's far.
  4. Manage: stop = Safety Line (close through it = out); move it as new swing points form; add to the position as the trend continues. No fixed profit target in her playbook.

What our tests did NOT capture: the coded version (tori_trendline_lab.pine, trendline_break) draws lines on one timeframe from 5-bar pivots, with only an optional daily-EMA filter — no higher-timeframe structure (HH/HL) bias, no thick hand-drawn lines, and both setups taken regardless of the bigger trend. So the results in section 7 test the mechanical core, not her full top-down method. Note: HTF uptrend + pullback + break is close to the weekly pullback strategy that did pass in my backtests.

1. The idea in one line

Draw two lines on the chart: the Action Line tells you when to enter, the Safety Line tells you where you're wrong (the stop). No indicators.

2. Step 1 — find swing points (pivots)

  • Swing high = a candle whose high is the highest of the 5 candles on each side. Swing low = lowest low of 5 on each side.
  • A swing point is only confirmed 5 candles later (you need the 5 candles after it) — so every line is drawn a little late.

3. Step 2 — draw the lines

  • Support line = straight line through the last two swing lows. Rising support = uptrend.
  • Resistance line = straight line through the last two swing highs. Falling resistance = downtrend.
  • Line price at any candle b: line(b) = p1 + (p2 − p1) / (b2 − b1) × (b − b1) — the slope is the trend's velocity (see price_physics_basics.md).
  • 3-touch line: an older (third) swing point also sits on the line, within 0.3 × ATR ("thick line" tolerance).

4. Step 3 — the two setups (long side; shorts are the mirror image)

Break (the one that works)

  • Entry: a candle closes above a falling resistance line while the previous close was below it.
  • Safety Line (stop): the rising support line if there is one below price, otherwise the last swing low.
  • Skip the trade if the stop is too far: entry − safety > 3 × ATR (Tori's "don't chase breaks far from the safety line" — the best rule in the system).
  • Risk R = entry − safety. Optional target at 2R or 3R.
  • First touch of the line must be ≥ 7 days old; each line can trigger only one trade.

Bounce (doesn't work in tests)

  • Entry: price dips to a rising support line (third touch, within 0.3 ATR) and closes back above it.
  • Stop: a close below the line.

5. Step 4 — managing the trade

  • Exit when a candle closes below the stop line (not just a wick).
  • Trail: each time a new higher swing low forms, move the stop up — to the rising support line, or to the new swing low, whichever is higher.
  • Optional fixed 2R / 3R target.

6. Worked example (break)

  • Swing highs: ₹1,000 at candle 0 and ₹950 at candle 20 → slope = −2.5 per candle. At candle 30 the line is at ₹925.
  • Candle 29 closed ₹920 (line there ₹927.5 → below). Candle 30 closes ₹930 (above ₹925) → break → buy ₹930.
  • Last swing low ₹900 → stop ₹900 → risk ₹30 = 1R. ATR ₹15 → 30 is 2 × ATR ≤ 3 × ATR → trade allowed.
  • 2R target = 930 + 60 = ₹990. With ₹10L and 1% risk: ₹10,000 ÷ ₹30 = 333 shares.

7. What the tests showed

TradingView tests (13 stocks + Nifty, long only, 0.12% per side; tori_multistock_playbook.md):

TimeframeWin rate (Break only)Profit factorProfitable symbols
15-min20%0.510/13 — loses even before costs
1-hour34%0.845/13
4-hour37%1.319/13 (edge faded after 2021)
Daily43% (51.5% with a 2R target)1.9012/13 (13/13 with 2R target)
  • Break works, Bounce doesn't (Bounce lost or broke even on every timeframe).
  • On 4-hour, a MACD histogram > 0 filter helped; on daily no indicator helped.
  • Almost never beat buy-and-hold (0 of 13 on daily) — it sits in cash much of the time.

Portfolio test (Nifty 200, Break only, 1% risk + ATR stop; trading-equation-backtests/reports/REPORT.md), 2022–Oct 2026: weekly 12–16% a year (Sharpe 0.56–0.69; the 200-day market filter cut its drawdown from 15% to 9%), daily 8–12% (Sharpe 0.16–0.39), 1-hour and intraday lost. Equal-weight hold of the same stocks: 18.9% a year.

8. Why it behaves like this

  • A break of a falling line = the downtrend's velocity flips — the start of a new move (momentum). That has a real, if small, edge.
  • A bounce bets that a line drawn through two noisy points will hold a third time — on automatic lines it usually doesn't.
  • On short timeframes swing points are mostly noise and costs are large relative to the moves.
  • Lines are drawn late (5-candle confirmation), so entries are not at the bottom.

9. If I use it

Daily (or weekly) chart · Break only · skip breaks > 3 ATR from the Safety Line · 1% risk per trade · trail the Safety Line or take 2R–3R · only when Nifty is above its 200-day average · spread across 10–15 liquid stocks · compare with an index fund.
